html:
The Navajo, or Diné, are an Indigenous people of the Southwest, now the largest tribal nation in the United States. Their language belongs to the Southern Athabaskan family, which shows their ancestors came south from the far north, reaching the Southwest a century or two before 1500.

They learned farming and weaving from the Pueblos, and after the Spanish arrived they took up sheep and horses. Wool weaving and herding became the heart of Navajo life. They raided and traded with Spanish and Pueblo settlements for two centuries.

In 1863 to 1864 the US army under Kit Carson burned their fields and drove some 8,000 Navajo on the Long Walk to Bosque Redondo in New Mexico, where many died. The Treaty of 1868 let them return home, and their reservation grew into the vast Navajo Nation of Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. In the Second World War Navajo code talkers sent radio messages in their language that the Japanese never broke. See Diné Bikéyah and the Navaho of the 1500s.
